blogs.title: When Anaphylaxis Comes Back Again: Managing Biphasic and Multiphasic Relapse in the ED and ICU
blogs.description: This post would use the case to explore the practical challenge of distinguishing true biphasic or multiphasic anaphylaxis from refractory anaphylaxis, transient epinephrine response, or ongoing allergen absorption. It would review current definitions, why they matter clinically, and how relapse timing should influence disposition, escalation to ICU-level monitoring, and bedside reassessment.

blogs.title: 0.3 mg Isn’t 0.5 mg: Are We Underdosing Adult Anaphylaxis?
blogs.description: This post would focus on epinephrine dosing in adults, using this 104 kg patient to highlight the gap between guideline-recommended 0.5 mg intramuscular dosing and the common real-world use of 0.3 mg auto-injectors. It would discuss how convenience and speed favor auto-injectors, but also how underdosing may contribute to repeat dosing, escalation of care, and persistent hemodynamic instability.

blogs.title: Observation After Anaphylaxis: Who Needs 4 Hours, Who Needs 24?
blogs.description: This post would examine the unresolved question of post-anaphylaxis observation time. Using the patient’s repeated relapses within 12 hours, it would discuss the limitations of fixed observation windows, summarize risk factors associated with biphasic reactions, and argue for a more risk-stratified approach that balances patient safety against unnecessary admissions and resource use.

blogs.title: Steroids in Anaphylaxis: Tradition, Inertia, and the Evidence Gap
blogs.description: This post would analyze why corticosteroids are still commonly given in anaphylaxis despite increasingly weak evidence for preventing biphasic reactions. The case is ideal for discussing how protocol variation, clinician habit, and fear of recurrence sustain steroid use, and how educators can help teams align practice with modern guideline recommendations while acknowledging lingering uncertainty in severe cases.

blogs.title: The Hidden Mast Cell Problem: When Recurrent Anaphylaxis Should Trigger a Mastocytosis Workup
blogs.description: This post would focus on the downstream diagnostic implications of unusually severe or recurrent anaphylaxis. It would review when elevated baseline tryptase, recurrent episodes, or atypical severity should prompt evaluation for systemic mastocytosis or other mast cell disorders, and how such conditions may alter counseling, follow-up, and long-term risk assessment even when formal diagnostic criteria are not fully met.

blogs.title: Tryptase Timing Matters: Getting the Lab Work Right in Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: This post would turn the case’s imperfect tryptase sampling into a teaching opportunity about diagnostic workflow. It would cover when tryptase is useful, the recommended sequence of acute and baseline samples, common reasons samples are missed in real-world emergency care, and how better systems can improve diagnostic yield without delaying time-critical treatment.
